Abstract
Ion transport across biological lipid membranes is crucial for both health and disease, prompting
investigation into synthetic ion transporters as potential therapeutics. However, state of the art
methods for assessing transporter activity are often time-consuming and resource-intensive,
hindering the screening of large compound libraries. In this work we have developed an
automated high-throughput assay capable of determining 24 EC50 values in a single day. This
assay, adapted from the established lucigenin Cl-/NO3- antiport method, has been optimised for
multi-well plates with fully automated liquid handling. Notably, our protocol allows for the use
of DMSO as a delivery solvent for target molecules, enhancing its versatility. Validation with six
standard ion transporters demonstrated a strong correlation between the EC50 values obtained
through our assay and previously reported values, conﬁrming its eﬃcacy and potential for
broader applications in the ﬁeld of ion transport.
Keywords
ion transport, automation, high throughput, ﬂuorescence, vesicle

Abstract 
Ion transport across biological lipid membranes is crucial for both health and disease, pr ompting 
investigation into synthetic ion transporters as potential therapeutics. However, state of the art methods 
for assessing transporter activity are often time -consuming and resource -intensive, hindering the 
screening of large compound libraries. In this work we have developed an automated high -throughput 
assay capable of determining 24 EC50 values in a single day. This assay, adapted from the established 
lucigenin Cl-/NO3- antiport method, has been optimised  for multi-well plates with fully automated liquid 
handling. Notably, our protocol allows for the use of DMSO as a delivery solvent for target molecules, 
enhancing its versatility. Validation with six standard ion transporters demonstrated a strong correlation 
between the E C50 values obtained through our assay and previously reported values, confirming its 
efficacy and potential for broader applications in the field of ion transport. 
Introduction 
Synthetic ion transporters play a crucial role in the translocation of ions across the phospholipid bilayer, 
and their biological applications have been investigated for the treatment of channelopathies, cancer, 
and microbial infections. [1–21] Despite their therapeutic potential, predicting the ion -transport efficiency 
of novel receptors remains challenging. Previous efforts to address this issue have included quantitative 
structure-activity relationship (QSAR) studies involving extensive transporter libraries aimed at 
developing predictive models; however, these appro aches are often time-consuming and costly under 
current methodologies.[22] Notably, the Hill analysis —commonly employed to determine the E C50 as a 
quantitative measure of transport efficacy—requires significant time investment, typically allowing only 
one transporter to be assessed per researcher per day. Furthermore, repeat experiments are 
infrequently conducted, and the reproducibility of results is often unexplored. The associated time and 
financial constraints can be particularly limiting for smaller research groups or those with restricted 
funding, potentially hindering commercialisation efforts.

In contrast, high-throughput experimentation has transformed the pharmaceutical sector, [23] yet to our 
knowledge, no high -throughput methods currently exis t for assessing anion transport activity. Such 
methodologies hold great promise for alleviating the experimental bottlenecks associated with 
traditional assays, enhancing time efficiency, and enabling the evaluation of more extensive compound 
libraries, wh ich can lead to quicker hit identification and more comprehensive structure -activity 
relationship studies. There is an increasing trend towards the integration of automated workflows as 
cost-effective and productivity -enhancing strategies within medicinal chemistry, fuelled by 
advancements in automated synthesis, purification, and biological assessment. [24] 
In this work, we present the design of high-throughput anion antiport assays that significantly enhance 
the throughput of ion transport workflows. We have  adapted the established lucigenin assay [25] into 
high-throughput formats utilising commonly accessible fluorescence plate reader technology. Initially, 
we developed a manual preparation method for a 96 -well plate format using multi -channel pipettes, 
followed by creating semi -automated and automated workflows for 384 -well plates employing the 
Opentrons OT -2 liquid handling platform. Our assays have been benchmarked against literature 
compounds previously evaluated via ion-selective electrode assays, demonstrating a strong correlation 
(R² = 0.99 - 0.89). This publication aims to provide detailed methodologies and the necessary files for 
plate-reader setup and data analysis, thereby making these methods accessible to other researchers. 
We anticipate that these techniques will facilitate the rapid evaluation of extensive compound libraries, 
enabling future studies to explore a wider chemical space and align more closely with the methodologies 
favoured by the pharmaceutical industry. 
Results and Discussion 
Ion transport is typically measured using ion -selective electrode assays or fluorescence assays, and 
we determined that the latter would be more suitable for adaptation to a high -throughput format. The 
lucigenin assay, a well -established method in the field, q uantifies direct chloride transport across 
synthetic vesicle membranes, which are usually composed of 1 -palmitoyl-2-oleoyl-glycero-3-
phosphocholine (POPC) or POPC/cholesterol mixtures.[25] These vesicles contain NaNO3 and lucigenin 
(N,N’-dimethyl-9,9’-biacridiniumdinitrate), a fluorescent sensor that is quenched by chloride ions in a 
concentration-dependent manner, as described by the Stern -Volmer equation ( equation S1 ). The 
assay begins with the addition of NaCl to the external buffer of  the vesicles, allowing the anion 
transporter to facilitate passive chloride influx via a Cl ⁻/NO3⁻ antiport mechanism, leading to 
fluorescence quenching. The fluorescence intensity can be calibrated against reference measurements; 
typically, 0% influx corresponds to the initial fluorescence shortly after the NaCl spike, while 100% influx 
is represented by the fluorescence reading obtained after adding detergent or a highly effective 
transporter.[26,27] Various data processing methods can then be employed to quantify transport activity, 
such as calculating the EC50 or the specific initial rate.[25] 
The E C50 is commonly reported as a measure of transport activity. It reflects  the the oretical 
concentration of an anionophore required to achieve 50% ion influx or eff lux by the end of the assay. 
This value is determined from a Hill plot, which is created by plotting the final chloride influx against 
transporter concentration. Traditionally, these experiments are performed individually in a cuvette or 
single vial, typically testing 6-8 different transporter concentrations in triplicate. As a result, this standard 
protocol usually allows for the assessment of only one compound per day due to time limitations.  
To establish a high -throughput (HT) Hill plot assay in a 96 -well plate format, we made several 
adaptations to existing protocols. While the traditional lucigenin assay continuously records 
fluorescence, the Hill plot only requires an end -point reading; thus, we focused on optimising the 
accuracy of this single measure ment, which was taken five minutes after NaCl addition. Another key 
objective was to develop an assay compatible with DMSO as a delivery solvent for the anion transporter. 
DMSO is widely used in other ion transport assays due to its ability to dissolve a b road range of poorly 
soluble transporters, but it is rarely incorporated into the lucigenin assay because it is known to quench 
lucigenin fluorescence. Our investigations revealed that the assay could tolerate small amounts of 
DMSO (as long as the concentration was consistent across wells), with fluorescence partially quenched 
at 1% v/v. Notably, an intravesicular chloride concentration of 100 mM resulted in a six-fold fluorescence 
quenching response, even in the presence of 1% DMSO, and the Stern -Volmer plot remained linear 
https://doi.org/10.26434/chemrxiv-2024-kxf0x ORCID: https://orcid.org/0000-0003-4262-8560 Content not peer-reviewed by ChemRxiv. License: CC BY 4.0

from 0 -100 mM [Cl ⁻] under assay conditions ( Supplementary Figure S28 ). Therefore, by carefully 
controlling the DMSO concentration and the ionic gradients, we successfully utilised DMSO as a 
delivery solvent for our transporters. 
The optimised assay protocol is outlined in Figure 1  and involves the following steps: 1) Vesicles 
containing encapsulated lucigenin were added to each well o f a 96 -well plate using a multi -channel 
pipette (150 L per well, 2 mM POPC, internal buffer = 100 µM lucigenin in 200 mM NaNO 3 with 5 mM 
sodium phosphate buffer, pH 7.2. External buffer = 200 mM NaNO3 with 5 mM sodium phosphate buffer, 
pH 7.2.). Then a sol ution of transporter in DMSO was added to the lipid, followed by mixing using a 
multi-channel pipette (3 µL of 100X stock solution). 2) Analysis was performed on a plate reader 
equipped with an autoinjector, which facilitated the addition of a sodium chloride spike to each well (150 
µL per well, 200 mM NaCl, with 5 mM sodium phosphate buffer, pH 7.2). 3) The fluorescence emission 
intensity (excitation = 369 nm, emission = 503 nm) of each well was measured 5 minutes after the 
addition of the sodium chloride,  and this was processed to give the final Hill plots. Data processing 
included the creation of a Stern-Volmer plot (Figure S28), which was used to convert the fluorescence 
intensity to a chloride concentration. It is important to note that up to 20% lucige nin leakage from the 
vesicles may occur within two hours,[25] which should not be confused with ion transport. Additional data 
calibration was performed using vesicles treated with DMSO only as a reference for 0% chloride influx 
and a highly potent transporter as a reference for 100% chloride influx (Equation S2). 
 
 
Figure 1. An overview of the steps involved in the high-throughput screening of ion-transporters via 
the lucigenin assay. This involves adding the transporter solutions to the vesicles and mixing, then 
adding sodium chloride to the external buffer to begin the assay. The end-point measurements were 
timed at 5 minutes after the injection of the spike. 
 
To validate our assay, we aimed to obtain the E C50 values for known compounds and compare them 
with literature values. A library of six established ion transporters ( 1–6, as shown in Figure 2) were 
synthesised as standards. This library includes anion transporters from various structural classes (such 
as ureas, thioureas, and squaramides) with reported E C50 values spanning three orders of magnitude 
(from 0.005 to 10 mol% with respect to lipid) .[22, 28, 31]  The chloride -nitrate antiport activity of these 
transporters was previously assessed using ion-selective electrode assays.

Figure 2.The compound library, their reported EC50 and the EC50 found via the high throughput 
assays 
 
The compound library was initially screened using 96-well plates, and we conducted three Hill plots for 
each of the compounds 1–6 (Figure 3). To evaluate the reproducibility and experimental error of our 
measurements, each Hill plot for a specific compound was performed with a differ ent batch of vesicles 
on separate plates. The EC50 values obtained by this method correlated strongly with literature values 
(R² = 0.99). 
With the initial method established, we focused on automating the most labour -intensive aspect of the 
assay: the preparation of the multi -well plates. The final composition of each well was standardised, 
and all volumes were scaled down to one-third to accommodate the smaller capacity of 384-well plates 
compared to 96-well plates. We developed a liquid dispensing protocol using the Opentrons OT-2 liquid 
handling robot, with the goal of minimising pipetting errors and enhancing data throughput by utilising 
384-well plates. The protocols were crafted using the Opentrons Protocol Designer, and the method 
files are provided as supplementary material to this article. 
The automation process was implemented in stages. Initially, we created a semi -automated protocol 
that allowed the Opentrons to dispense pre-mixed lipid and transporter solutions into the 384-well 
plate. Subsequently, we developed a fully automated method where the Opentrons performed all 
liquid handling steps, including diluting transporter stock solutions in DMSO, mixing the transporter 
solutions with the lipid, and dispensing these mixtures into the 384-well plates. Detailed standard 
operating procedures for each method, along with relevant instrument settings and data analysis 
spreadsheets, are available in the supplementary materials.

Figure 3: Compiled Hill plots for compounds 1–6. Black curves represent results from the manual HT 
lucigenin assay where 3 repeated Hill plots were performed in 3 different batches of vesicles. Error bars 
represent standard deviation. (b) Red curves represent results from the semi-automated method where 
4 repeated Hill plots were obtained from lipid and transporter solutions that were prepared by hand, and 
automatically dispensed into the plate. (c) Blue curves repre sent results from the automated method 
where 4 repeated Hill plots were obtained, and all pipetting was performed by the Opentrons.  
 
The manual 96-well plate method exhibited the greatest variation in results, likely due to inconsistencies 
in manual pipetting and batch-to-batch variability among the vesicle samples. The standard deviations 
of the three EC50 values derived from replicate Hill plots for each compound ranged from 8% to 37% of 
the mean value (Figure 4a). While repeat Hill plots are infrequently reported in the literature, these error 
margins align with the variability observed in a large compound library assessed using ion -selective 
electrode assays, which reported errors between 9% and 38%. [22] These findings underscore the 
inherent variability in E C50 measurements across experiments, highlighting the necessity for efficient 
protocols to facilitate repeat experiments. 
Compounds 2 and 5 emerged as the most challenging ionophores  to study  within our series. For 
compound 5, the highest loadings (>0.02 mol% w.r.t. lipid) resulted in unexpectedly low transport 
activity (Figure S30), necessitating the exclusion of these data points for fitting to the Hill equation. Our 
EC50 values for compound 5 were the least reproducible, with errors reaching up to 38%, while  the 
largest discrepancy between literature and high -throughput (HT) E C50 values was observed for 
compound 2. We attribute these issues to difficulties in delivering these compounds to the vesicle 
bilayer. The low transport activity of compound 2 required testing at very high concentrations, which 
could have resulted in aggregation. Additionally, squaramides like compound 5 are poorly soluble in 
solvents other than DMSO due to the potential for intermolecular hydrogen bonding.  [28–30] Previous 
studies have indicated that more dilute stock solutions of compound 5 in DMSO exhibit higher transport 
activity, suggesting a challenge in delivering this compound effectively. [28] While co-delivery with larger 
volumes of DMSO could enhance delivery into the bilaye r, this approach is incompatible with our HT 
assay, which requires a constant DMSO volume to maintain consistent fluorescence quenching. 
Another significant distinction between our assay and the ion-selective electrode assay is the absence 
of stirring while adding the transporter solution. We hypothesise that the lack of stirring may exacerbate 
https://doi.org/10.26434/chemrxiv-2024-kxf0x ORCID: https://orcid.org/0000-0003-4262-8560 Content not peer-reviewed by ChemRxiv. License: CC BY 4.0

delivery issues. Further investigation of deliverability is critical for the potential biological applications, 
as some poorly deliverable ion transporters that demonstrate high activity in vesicle studies may show 
poor activity in cells.[14] 
Overall, we have developed analogues of this assay with varying levels of automation. Figure 4 
illustrates the results from the manual, semi-automated, and fully automated HT methods, showing 
good agreement with literature values. The correlations between HT and literature E C50 values are 
visually represented, with R² values of 0.99, 0.98, and 0.89 for the manual, semi -automated, and 
automated methods, respectively. These strong correlations indicate that the HT assay produces 
accurate EC50 data comparable to that obtained through traditional methods. 
 
Figure 4: (a) A summary of the EC50 values determined via our high-throughput assay and (b) a visual 
representation of the HT E C50 values plotted against the literature E C50 values. Labels represent the 
compound tested, and is placed above or below the relevant data points. Error bars show the standard 
deviation of 3 repeats for the manual method, and the standard deviation of 4 experimental repeats for 
the semi-automated and automated methods. The R2 values are shown in the legend. 
 
Our methods demonstrate significant potential to save time and enhance data generation within anion 
transport workflows. Using the manual 96 -well method, we were able to prepare up to six plates in a 
single day, yielding a total of 18 Hill plots. In contrast, conventional procedures for generating Hill plots 
typically allow for only one plot to be collected per day. The use of a plate reader streamlines th e 
process, enabling the addition of sodium chloride followed by fluorescence measurement to be 
completed in approximately 10 minutes per 96-well plate. 
The most time-consuming and labour-intensive aspect of this assay was the pipetting, prompting us to 
optimise this further. Our fully automated method allowed us to collect 24 Hill plots in a single day. Each 
384-well plate required approximately two hours for preparation in a fully automated process that does 
not require researcher intervention after the method started, followed by 30 minutes for assessment on 
the plate reader to generate 12 Hill plots. Future improvements may be achievable by incorporating a 
liquid-handling robot equipped with multi-channel pipettes. This would facilitate the batch-wise addition 
of pre -prepared DMSO solutions to the vesicle -containing plates. This would not only expedite the 
addition of transporter solutions but also increase the number of plates prepared daily while minimising 
lipid degradation, given that the vesicles should be used within 2-3 hours. However, we did not explore 
this on the Opentrons OT -2 due to concerns about instrumental error for low -volume transfers, as the 
reported accuracy of the 8 -channel GEN2 pipettes at 1 µL is ±20%. Maintaining the DMSO 
https://doi.org/10.26434/chemrxiv-2024-kxf0x ORCID: https://orcid.org/0000-0003-4262-8560 Content not peer-reviewed by ChemRxiv. License: CC BY 4.0

concentration at a precise 1% v/v is crucial, as any variation could interfere with results due to DMSO's 
quenching properties. 
Conclusion 
In conclusion, we have developed high -throughput methodologies for quantifying chloride/nitrate 
antiport activity using a lucige nin assay. Validation with six previously characterised anionophores 
demonstrated that the E C50 values obtained were consistent with literature reports. Notably, these 
methods significantly reduce the time required compared to traditional approaches, and the integration 
of the Opentrons robotic liquid handling system enhances efficiency while minimising user error, making 
our protocols accessible to researchers with varying levels of experience.  
To our knowledge, this represents the first high-throughput approach for conducting a Hill plot 
analysis of anion transport. Our assay provides a foundation for further advancements in high-
throughput methodologies. Given the current intense research interest in ion transporter design, we 
hope that our methods will accelerate the pace of discovery and translation in this area.  The 
enhanced capacity for data generation will allow for the exploration of larger anionophore libraries. 
This broader exploration of chemical space will contribute to a deeper understanding of structure -
activity relationships and aid in the identification of new design principles. By making these high -
throughput methods accessible to the research community, we aim to alleviate the exp erimental 
bottleneck in ionophore screening, ultimately advancing research and facilitating the discovery of 
novel biologically active transporters.
